Chapter 26

The trip page: one await, one state object, one stream

The page awaits tripBySlug in markup with no boundary; TripView starts the live query and reads props once with untrack; TripState derives everything from whichever snapshot is newer; two presence effects that must not loop; tabs from the URL.

By the end of this chapter

Build a page whose first paint comes from one query and whose every later paint comes from a live stream, with local interaction state kept apart from server state.

This is the page everything else hangs off, and it is short because the work is elsewhere. The page awaits one remote query; the view starts the live one; the state object derives every value the tabs read; and the tabs are components that take the state object as a prop.

One await, in the markup, with no boundary. The comment says why twice over: a pending snippet is what the server would render *instead of* the trip, so the first paint would be a placeholder and a second request; and the failure that matters is a 404, which belongs to +error.svelte with the right status and language — where an uncaught error from a remote function goes. The await sits inside $derived in a declaration tag, so initial follows the slug and the query; a bare {const} is worked out once, and would go on holding the first trip it was given. {#key slug} makes a different trip a fresh TripView, which is what lets the view read its props once.

Why params from the props, and not page.params

A page receives its route’s parameters as a prop, params, and PageProps from ./$types is the type SvelteKit generates for exactly this route: params.slug is a string, already accepted by the matcher in src/params.ts (chapter 15), because a URL whose slug did not match never reached this file. page.params from $app/state holds the same value as global state, typed for every route in the app at once — so on that type slug may be missing, and the first version wrote page.params.slug ?? '', a fallback that could never run and that would have sent an empty string to a query whose schema refuses it. The prop is also what makes the page an ordinary component: what it depends on is in its signature. SvelteKit’s documentation shows the same pair for the same reason — let { params } = $props() beside a remote query called with params.slug.

The state object

Two kinds of thing, kept apart. What the server says — the document — is derived from whichever is newer: the live query’s latest snapshot, or the first paint’s document until the stream delivers. What this person is doing — the selected stop — is local $state that is never sent anywhere. (The open tab is not here at all: it lives in the URL, and the view below derives it from there.) Everything else is $derived from the two, so a change on the server or a click on the screen re-derives exactly the parts that depend on it. The $derived.by closures are there because the private fields are assigned in the constructor, after field initialisers run; the comment explains the TypeScript reason.

Why a class and not a store, or a context

A class with $state and $derived fields is the Svelte 5 shape for “an object several components read from”. It is typed, it has methods, it can be constructed with arguments, and every field is fine-grained — a component that reads view.total re-renders when the total changes and not when the presence list does. A store would make every consumer subscribe to everything; a context would hide the dependency. Passing view as a prop is explicit, and Itinerary, Expenses, Notes and Companions all take exactly that.

The view

watchTrip(slug) is the live query; .current is the latest snapshot and .connected says whether the stream is up. It is created inside untrack, and so is the state object, because the props are read once on purpose — the page keys this component on the slug — and untrack both says so and quiets the compiler’s fair question. The tab comes from the URL: ?tab=map is a link, so it works with the back button, can be shared, and needs no state. What the URL says is a string | null, and isTab from state.svelte.ts is a type guard — value is Tab — so the value that passes it is a Tab to TypeScript with no cast, and anything else falls back to the itinerary.

Read the comment above the effects slowly; it records two bugs the end-to-end suite found, and both are general. First, an effect that read view.trip re-ran every time the live query yielded — because view.trip is a new object each time — and its cleanup said goodbye, which woke the room, which yielded, which re-ran the effect: a loop through the server. The id is a string that never changes, so it is read once. Second, a remote command keeps a little reactive state of its own and reads it as it starts; called inside an effect, that read becomes a dependency and the write that follows re-runs the effect synchronously until Svelte stops it with effect_update_depth_exceeded. untrack around the call says: run this, depend on nothing it touches.

The general rule: an $effect should read the reactive values it *reacts to* and nothing else. Anything it merely *uses* — a remote function, a library call that keeps state, a derived object you only need one field of — goes inside untrack, or is read once outside the effect. The Svelte MCP autofixer flags every function call inside an effect for exactly this reason; most are fine, and the ones that are not are loops.

The heartbeat and the goodbye are sent and not awaited, and the first version wrote .catch(() => {}) after each — reasonable for a heartbeat, whose next attempt is fifteen seconds away, and exactly how a real bug hid for an afternoon: when the seeded ids turned out not to be UUIDs (chapter 14), every heartbeat that named a seeded stop failed validation on the server and nobody heard. fireAndForget() keeps the production behaviour — nothing a person could act on — and adds a console warning in development, where somebody is looking. Silence is a decision; it should be one you can see in the code.

The header shows the live status, in four states rather than two: a pulsing chip while the stream is up, a quiet “Connecting…” for the first three seconds while it is not up *yet*, and only after that the coral “Reconnect” button — live.reconnect() is the method SvelteKit gives every live query. The first version had two states, and showed “Reconnect” the moment the page hydrated, before the stream had had a chance: everybody on a slow network was told something had failed when nothing had. The fourth state comes first in the derivation: when the device itself has no network, the chip says “Offline” in the same quiet grey and offers nothing, because a button that cannot work is a button that lies — chapter 39 is where a page with no network comes from, and why the stream needs asking back. All four share one slot as wide as the widest label, so the palette and settings beside it never move. The width comes from an invisible sizer in the same grid cell whose labels are generated text — content: attr(data-label) — so they are in nobody’s way: not in the accessibility tree, not in the page’s text, not a second “Live” for a test to find. The slot is that wide and the chip is not: a grid item stretches to its cell by default, and “Live” sat in a pill two and a half times its width, crowded to one side. justify-self puts the chip at the slot’s leading edge on a phone, where the tools read from the left, and at its trailing edge beside the name, where they are set against the right — so the edge beside the settings button is the one that stays put when the label changes.

On a phone the trip’s name has the full width and the status tools are a row of their own under the lede; from 40em they move up beside the name. Sharing the name’s row at every width, as the first version did, left a real trip name 177px of a 328px column, and “A long weekend in the Douro valley with the cousins” ran to five ragged lines of display type. On a phone the palette button is a magnifier and the settings link an icon, its word still its name, visually hidden.

The strip itself. The tabs are links to the same route with a different ?tab= — href() with a route id that carries its search string — marked data-sveltekit-reset="false" so the scroll position and the focus survive the navigation; SvelteKit 3 folded the old noscroll and keepfocus attributes into that one reset, and only warns about the old names in development, it no longer reads them. The strip is sticky under the header, so the tabs stay in reach down a long itinerary, and it scrolls sideways on a phone, where six tabs do not fit. The frame around it carries the paper and two edge fades, ::before and ::after gradients from --paper to transparent, each shown only while there is more strip that way. The first version faded the strip with a mask-image, which faded whatever was *behind* the strip too — the page scrolling under a sticky element — and faded the current tab whenever it sat at an edge.

One bar slides under the current tab instead of each link drawing its own border, and its position is a Tween from svelte/motion: a value that, when set, moves to the new one over a duration, with .current read by the markup on every frame. The effect reads tab and so re-runs on every switch; the first set passes { duration: 0 } so the bar starts under the tab rather than sliding in from the edge, and reduced motion — read with untrack, because the effect should not re-run when the setting changes — makes every move instant. The second effect is a ResizeObserver on the strip and on every link: a rotation, a resize or a late font changes a tab’s width, and the bar is measured again — moved, not animated, because nothing was chosen. The current tab is also scrolled into view by hand, to a position that leaves 32px clear on either side, because scrollIntoView({ inline: 'nearest' }) stops exactly at the strip’s edge, which is where the fade is: “Notes” was left with its last letter and its bar faded out. And there is no scroll snapping — proximity snapping took a tab scrolled into view by hand and re-aligned it to the edge, under the fade again. The bar sits inside the strip — overflow-y: hidden, the hairline under the tabs an inset shadow — because a scroll container clips at its padding box: a bar placed on the border was cut to 1px and let the strip scroll a pixel up and down.

The map and the globe fill what is left of the screen below the tabs, so their bottom edge — the map’s status pill, the globe’s “Fly the route” — is on screen without a scroll, at 1440×900 and on a phone alike. A fixed 72dvh did not manage that, because how much is left depends on the header, and the header depends on the trip’s name, the width and the language. So the effect measures the panel’s top in page coordinates whenever the header changes size, writes it to --frame-top, and the CSS does the rest: clamp(20rem, calc(100dvh - var(--frame-top, var(--frame-guess)) - var(--space-4)), 46rem). Until the script has measured — on the server, and in the first frame — the top is --frame-guess, a guess for the width: 21rem on a phone, where the status tools are a row of their own, 18rem beside them from 40em. A guess that matches the measurement is a frame that does not change height under a map that has already started, which the map in chapter 29 had to be taught to survive.

The panel has a view-transition-name of its own, so a tab switch cross-fades the panel while the header and the strip hold still. The itinerary tab is a split view from 64em, with the map sticky beside the days, and the list alone below that — the Map tab is one tap away. The map is not hidden with CSS on a phone but not rendered at all: wide is a MediaQuery, and a hidden MapLibre would still be a WebGL context, two of them for one trip on the device least able to afford it. Both components take the same view and the same callbacks, and selecting a stop in one highlights it in the other because the selection lives in view.

Checkpoint

  • You can say why the trip page has no pending snippet and where a 404 goes.
  • You can say why the slug comes from params through PageProps rather than from page.params.
  • You can explain what TripState.document is derived from and what that means for caching.
  • You can state the effect rule and identify both loops the presence effects avoid.
